item.title: Heat on construction sites: SSIC calls for an end to penalties
item.description: The Swiss Society of Manufacturers and Entrepreneurs asks for fair conditions and exemptions from contractual penalties in the event of a stop to the work for the canicola.
item.content:encoded:
IN BRIEF
- The SSIC requests the abolition of penalties for delays in construction sites caused by heat.
- The heatwave is not considered equivalent to bad weather and lacks compensation.
- The Commission of the Council of States considers the parliamentary motion outdated.

KEY FACTS
- **What**: Petition for fair conditions in construction sites during heatwaves
- When: Parliamentary initiatives between December 2024 and March 2025
- Where: Construction sites throughout Switzerland
- Who: Swiss Society of Contractors (SSIC) and Parliament
- Amount: Contractual penalties of unspecified amount

During weeks characterized by intense heatwaves, the construction sector in Switzerland faces complex challenges related both to worker safety and to meeting project deadlines. The Swiss Society of Contractors (SSIC) has launched a petition aiming to request the introduction of fair and realistic framework conditions for managing work during extreme temperatures, asking that construction companies are not contractually penalized for the unavoidable delays caused by the heat.

The call for protection and clear rules
In the petition, the SSIC emphasizes the urgent need to ensure effective protection of the health of construction workers. Contractors request that realistic deadlines are set for the completion of works and that transparent and uniform rules are established in cases where work must be suspended due to high temperatures.

Unlike what usually happens with adverse weather events or bad weather, interruptions and delays caused by extreme heat are rarely considered in construction contracts. Currently, such circumstances do not benefit from specific compensation, leaving companies exposed to high financial penalties in case of failure to meet agreed deadlines. Since heatwaves cannot be predicted or controlled by either companies or workers, the SSIC considers it unfair to fully burden builders with the economic consequences of these natural events.

Furthermore, the need to adhere to very tight contractual deadlines risks increasing operational pressure on personnel, directly jeopardizing the physical safety of outdoor workers under the blazing sun. Companies seeking to protect their staff by suspending work face potential economic damage related to the enforcement of penalty clauses. To understand the economic context of wages in the sector, it is possible to consult the details on the [Swiss payslip](nav:payslip) and related national parameters. ### The parliamentary framework and the position of the committees

The issue of protection against risks related to extreme temperatures at construction sites has been a topic of discussion within the federal Parliament as well. A pending motion requests the Federal Council to adopt appropriate measures so that natural influences are obligatorily included in planning and executing construction work. The text provides that, in the presence of extreme heat, construction companies should have the option to temporarily suspend activities to protect employees' health, without facing the threat of contractual penalties.

This motion had received support from the National Council, which approved it in December 2024. The parliamentary branch expressed the intention to establish explicit legislative protection for companies and workers.

### The position of the Council of States and the Committee

In March 2025, the Committee for Economics and Taxes of the Council of States announced its opinion on the parliamentary act. While sharing the fundamental objectives related to safeguarding health and ensuring fair working conditions, the Committee pointed out that the situation is already being managed. In line with the position expressed by the federal government, it was clarified that several measures have been initiated within a roundtable involving all relevant social partners in the sector.

Consequently, the Committee recommended that the plenum of the Council of States reject the motion, considering it effectively outdated by ongoing negotiations between employers and workers' representatives. The evolution of the debate highlights how much the issue impacts the [labour market](nav:jobs) and the organization of construction sites in Switzerland.

The discrepancy between the position of the National Council and that of the Committee of the States reflects the complexity of balancing production needs, contractual responsibilities of the client, and the duty to protect workers exposed to severe weather conditions.

The dispute over heatwave management at construction sites highlights the need for companies to carefully assess climate risk management when drafting procurement contracts. In the absence of an official legislative change, the issue remains entrusted to direct contractual negotiations between clients and construction firms, as well as to agreements established within negotiations among social partners.

For construction companies and workers, the immediate priority is to adopt internal preventive measures and adjust working hours during the summer months. Currently discussed practices include reorganizing shifts during the cooler parts of the day, setting up adequate shaded areas, providing refreshing drinks, and temporarily halting the most strenuous tasks when temperatures exceed safety thresholds.

HOW TO PLAN SITE MANAGEMENT AND DEADLINES

To avoid contractual penalties, construction companies planning interventions during the summer months can follow some procedural guidelines:

- Pre-verify contractual clauses related to force majeure events or extraordinary weather influences.
- Accurately and promptly document extreme weather conditions detected at the site through official measurements.
- Inform project management and clients promptly about the need to suspend activities for health protection reasons.
- Stay updated on the outcomes of the social partners' roundtable to incorporate new sector directives as soon as they are defined.

- When: In effect according to federal and cantonal regulations
- Where: Territory of the Swiss Confederation
- Who: SEM and competent cantonal authorities
- Amount: Issuance fees set by individual Cantons

The residence permit system in Switzerland comprises different types established by federal authorities, including the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), and implemented at the cantonal level. Understanding the distinction between categories L, B, and C is essential for those intending to settle or work in the country, considering that Switzerland is not a member of the European Union or the European Economic Area, although it applies specific bilateral agreements. Regulations precisely define access requirements, validity periods, and renewal procedures for each type of document issued to foreign citizens. Administrative management directly involves the population services of the various Cantons, which verify the applicant's economic, work, and housing conditions at the time of the initial application and during subsequent renewal deadlines. To learn more about the financial situation and deductions applied to salaries during the stay, you can consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) available online. ### The characteristics of short-term L permit

The L residence permit is intended for foreign citizens who have a fixed-term employment relationship, usually ranging from a few months to a year. This authorization is issued based on a specific employment contract, and its validity is strictly linked to the duration of the employment itself. Renewal of the L permit depends on the continued existence of the same employment conditions and does not automatically guarantee a transition to long-term residence categories. Procedurally, the employer or the worker must submit the required documentation to the cantonal migration office before starting professional activity on Swiss territory.

### The B residence permit for ordinary residence

The B residence permit represents authorization for ordinary residence, typically granted to those holding a permanent employment contract or a contract of at least one year's duration. The validity of this document is generally one year for third-country nationals and can be extended to five years for beneficiaries of the free movement agreements, depending on nationality and professional status. Holders of the B permit are required to comply with specific communication obligations in case of change of address or employment, promptly informing the relevant cantonal authorities. Unlike permit B, permit C is not tied to an annual expiry date and provides the holder with greater legal and economic stability, including exemption from certain restrictions regarding employment changes or independent activities. ## In brief

## Key facts
- **What**: Rights and obligations of tenants in Swiss leases
- When: Throughout the entire duration of the lease
- Where: Across the entire Swiss territory and in various cantons
- Who: Tenants, landlords, and competent conciliation authorities
- Amount: Security deposit up to a maximum of three months' net rent

The Swiss real estate market is regulated by precise federal and cantonal laws that define the legal framework for residential lease agreements. When renting an apartment in Switzerland, it is essential to thoroughly understand the regulations regarding notice periods, security deposits, and rent disputes to avoid legal conflicts with property owners or property management. These provisions apply uniformly at the federal level but have operational specifics related to different cantons. The Federal Statistical Office (BFS) regularly monitors the cost of living and rental prices, providing useful data to assess the appropriateness of the requested amounts.

### The security deposit and banking rules
Swiss law provides that the tenant may deposit an amount as security for contractual obligations up to a maximum of three months' net rent. This amount cannot be handed directly to the landlord but must be obligatorily deposited into a dedicated security deposit account opened in the tenant's name at a bank. This measure protects the tenant from improper use of the money and ensures that the interest accrued on the capital remains the property of the tenant throughout the lease duration. For more details on liquidity management and related accounts, see our [banking services](nav:banks).

### Contesting the initial rent
A fundamental right recognized by Swiss law concerns the possibility to contest the amount of the initial rent within a strict thirty-day period from the delivery of the property, if the amount is deemed abusive or generates excessive returns for the landlord. This verification is based on the criteria established by the Code of Obligations and considers the local real estate market context, the condition of the property, and the periodically published reference interest rates. Practical analysis of termination procedures and deadlines
Terminating a lease in Switzerland requires strict adherence to specific timeframes and formalities to avoid tacit renewal of the contract or the charging of unjustified monthly payments. The tenant's notice must be drafted exclusively in writing and signed by all parties listed on the lease agreement. In the case of an apartment occupied by a couple, the termination letter must bear the signatures of both spouses or registered partners, otherwise it is null and void.

The notice periods vary depending on the canton and local customs, although the Swiss Civil Code provides a minimum general term of three months for unfurnished apartments, with contractual deadlines established in individual agreements or according to cantonal practices. If the tenant intends to vacate the property before the contractual expiry without incurring financial penalties, law requires the presentation of at least one suitable, solvent substitute candidate willing to take over under the same contractual conditions on the same date.

### Return of the premises and the inspection report
At the time of vacating the property, the landlord and tenant jointly conduct an inspection of the premises to prepare the handover report. This document certifies the state of wear of the apartment and distinguishes normal signs of deterioration due to daily use from damages attributable to negligence or carelessness by the tenant. ## In a nutshell

## Key facts

- When: From 1 January 2026
- Where: Canton Ticino
- Who: Tax office at the source of Ticino, border workers residing in the new border municipalities
- Amount: Full rate (tables A, B, C, H) instead of 80% reduced

The Tax Office at the source of the Canton of Ticino has communicated, as reported by the Ocst union on its website, that from January 2026 the so-called "old border workers of the new Municipalities" who will opt for the mechanism of the Omnibus Decree will be taxed in Ticino at 100%, therefore according to the ordinary tables A, B, C and H, and no longer at 80% as is the case for new border workers.

### Who are the workers involved
The provision concerns workers who carried out activities in Ticino between 31 December 2018 and 17 July 2023 with daily return, maintaining tax residence in a municipality included within 20 kilometres of the border, but which did not appear in the old list of border municipalities of the Canton of Ticino. The Tax Office at source has decided to ### The change and its practical consequences
According to the OCST, with the new arrangement, affected cross-border workers would face a crossroads with significant economic implications. If they choose to opt for the Omnibus Decree, they will have to pay 100% of the withholding tax in Switzerland (according to full tables) and, at the same time, an additional amount in Italy as a substitute tax. The overall tax burden would be higher than the current situation.

The alternative would be not to opt for the Omnibus and continue paying 80% in Switzerland, while being classified as 'new cross-border workers.' This second option would avoid the immediate increase but would categorize the worker as a 'new cross-border worker' by legal definition, which does not match their contribution history (being an 'old' cross-border worker by seniority).

### Comparison of tax scenarios
| Scenario | Tax in Switzerland | Tax in Italy | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Old classic cross-border worker** | 100% (tables A,B,C,H) | Exempt | Historical regime |
| New cross-border worker (until 2025) | 80% reduced rates | 25% substitute tax on Swiss payments | Omnibus option |
| Old workers from new municipalities (from 2026 with Omnibus) | 100% (tables A,B,C,H) | 25% substitute tax | Increased burden |
| Old workers from new municipalities (from 2026 without Omnibus) | 80% reduced rates | None (ordinary regime?) | Classified as new cross-border worker |

The table highlights how the combination '100% in Switzerland + 25% in Italy' creates an imbalance compared to both the old classic cross-border workers (who pay only 100% in Switzerland) and their previous situation (80% + 25%).

### The OCST appeal and political timing
The Ticino union emphasizes that there is time until the end of 2026 to rectify the situation, but a structural solution to avoid increased taxes requires intervention from the Italian government with Bern to definitively resolve this 'ambiguous' situation that has persisted for several years. The matter is therefore on the diplomatic table between the two countries, with workers awaiting regulatory clarity that has yet to arrive.

### What changes for the income declaration
For affected cross-border workers, the choice between the two options will directly impact the preparation of the Italian tax return. Those opting for the Omnibus will need to indicate in box CE of model 730 (or Redditi PF) the Swiss withholding tax paid at 100% to claim the tax credit, while those remaining under the 80% regime will have a lower withholding tax amount to offset. The second pillar, known as professional pension or LPP, represents a fundamental pillar of the Swiss pension system together with AVS. Federal regulations establish that membership becomes mandatory upon reaching the 25th birthday for employees who exceed a certain annual salary threshold established by law. The system is based on an individual capitalization mechanism, where each worker accumulates a personal capital that will be paid out in the form of a lifelong annuity or capital at the time of retirement.

### Contribution rates and age ranges in professional pension
Contribution rates vary progressively based on the age of the insured person. Contribution rates start at 7% for the youngest age group that has just started the mandatory contribution obligation and gradually increase to 18% for workers in the more mature age ranges before retirement. These payments are deducted directly from the monthly salary and are divided between the employer and the employee, as provided for by the regulations of the pension fund company or collective.

### Management and administration of funds
Pension funds operate under the supervision of competent authorities and manage the pension fund assets, ensuring coverage against the risks of old age, disability and death. Statistics published by the Federal Statistical Office highlight the importance of this asset in the national economic framework. To deepen financial planning, residents can consult dedicated tools such as the [calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the impact on their economic situation. ### The redemption of contribution gaps

## In brief
- Mandatory LAMal insurance for those working or residing in Switzerland
- Right of option for cross-border workers between Italy and Switzerland
- Franchise rates for adults set between CHF 300 and CHF 2500

## Key points
- **What**: Mandatory health insurance LAMal
- When: 2026 for healthcare coverage
- Where: Swiss Confederation territory
- Who: UFSP/BAG, Cantons, and authorized sick funds
- Amount: Adult franchises from CHF 300 to CHF 2500

The Swiss healthcare system is based on principles of universality and obligation established by the federal law on health insurance (LAMal). Anyone engaged in an activity on the territory of the Helvetia or residing there is required to subscribe to a recognized insurance coverage. At the federal level, the Federal Office of Public Health (UFSP/BAG) oversees the application of the rules, while the Cantons manage the planning of healthcare and the accreditation of care structures. For cross-border workers who maintain their residence in Italy but work in Switzerland, the legislation provides the so-called right of option. This right allows, within the terms of the law, to choose whether to maintain the Swiss healthcare system through LAMal or to request exemption to join the Italian National Health Service. The choice, once exercised according to the provisions in force, has a generally definitive character for the entire period of cross-border working activity, except for specific exceptions regulated by bilateral treaties and agreements between Rome and Bern. The understanding of these mechanisms is fundamental for orienting oneself between costs and guaranteed performances. For a detailed analysis of the overall impact on the salary, consult [calculator](nav:calculator).

### Basic service structure
The LAMal guarantees access to a basket of basic medical services, which includes outpatient care provided by general practitioners and specialists, hospital treatments in the common ward of the home or work canton, and drugs listed in the official lists of the UFSP/BAG. Unlike fiscal health systems based on general taxation, the Swiss model requires the payment of fixed monthly premiums to the chosen sick fund, regardless of personal income. Cantons play a key role in authorizing sick funds and subsidizing public and private healthcare facilities. Residents and workers must carefully evaluate the different offers proposed by recognized sick funds, comparing the premiums applied at equal base coverage. The basic offer is identical by law at all recognized sick funds, but costs vary depending on the canton of residence or activity and the chosen insurance model, such as that with a family doctor or with obligatory telemedicine. ## Mandatory Analysis of Franchise and Cash Models

The financial management of one's health insurance coverage in Switzerland involves a deliberate choice of franchise and the supplementary or basic insurance model. The franchise represents the fixed annual medical expense that the insured must pay before the cash sick fund begins to reimburse the costs. For adults, the law provides ordinary or optional franchises that start at a minimum of 300 Swiss francs and can reach up to a maximum of 2500 Swiss francs per year. Choosing a high franchise reduces the monthly premium to be paid to the insurer but exposes to a higher financial risk in case of unexpected health problems and high medical expenses. On the other hand, a low franchise guarantees immediate reimbursements from the first medical expenses, albeit at the expense of much higher monthly premiums. Alongside the franchise, the insured must pay a participation quota, known as the percentage share, equal to 10% of the costs that exceed the franchise, up to an annual maximum set by federal law. The sick funds also propose alternative models that limit the free choice of the doctor at the beginning of the care path, offering in exchange discounts on premiums that can reach significant percentages. These models include the network of family doctors, telephone HMO centers, or contracted clinics.

### Choice of Cassa and Rights of Insured

The competition among the sick funds authorized by the UFSP/BAG allows insured individuals to change their sick fund or franchise model annually, in compliance with the deadlines and terms of termination set by federal law. The termination of the basic policy must be communicated to the current insurer within the term established, usually at the end of November to take effect from January 1st of the following year, provided that the insured does not have unpaid premiums. Before proceeding with the change, it is essential to verify that the new sick fund offers competitive tariffs and an adequate network of healthcare partners for one's working and personal needs. Health insurance companies cannot refuse the admission of any person to the mandatory basic health insurance, regardless of age or health status, and cannot apply health reserves on LAMal services. This guarantee of universal access protects workers and residents from discriminations related to pre-existing conditions. For those who need to manage the family budget between mandatory expenses and life costs, it is useful to evaluate the total monthly expenses through [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living).

The practical management of one's health coverage requires adherence to precise deadlines and the submission of the correct documentation to the competent authorities in Switzerland and the countries of origin, especially for those who frequently cross the border for professional reasons. Those who choose to exercise the right to opt for the Swiss system must submit a formal request to the competent cantonal authority within the terms set by the regulations, attaching documentation that confirms the employment status. For frontalier workers who opt for the LAMal, it is necessary to present the attestation of coverage to the Italian health authorities to regularize one's position and avoid double impositions or health assistance checks. The medical bills received from healthcare professionals must be paid directly by the insured and subsequently transmitted to their own sick fund through digital or postal channels provided by the insurer, attaching prescriptions and payment justifications. The refunds are made on the bank account indicated by the insured, after deducting the franchise and the percentage aliquot applicable. It is advisable to monitor constantly the communications sent by one's sick fund, especially in the fall months when adjustments to the premiums for the following year are announced. The annual financial planning must take into account these tariff increases, which vary depending on the canton and the overall evolution of the total healthcare costs reported by the federal offices. To verify the compatibility of the tax and pension contributions with the healthcare costs incurred, it is advisable to consult [calculator](nav:calculator).

### Periodic Compliance and Audits
The insured must promptly communicate any changes in their personal situation, such as a change of residence, a professional transfer to another canton, or a modification of the family nucleus. Any change of canton of residence or place of work may result in a review of the premiums applicable from the sick fund, as the tariffs are calculated on a cantonal basis. In case of disputes with the insurer regarding the refund of services or the application of the franchise, the insured can refer to the ombudsman for health insurance for an attempt at extrajudicial conciliation before initiating formal legal proceedings.
